[[File:Matthew linford teaching lecture.jpg|thumb|Matthew Linford leading a lecture]]
'''Matthew R. Linford''' (born April 9, 1966)<ref>''U.S. Public Records Index'' Vol 2 (Provo, Utah: Ancestry.com Operations, Inc.), 2010.</ref> is an American chemist and full professor in the Department of [[Chemistry]] and [[Biochemistry]] at [[Brigham Young University]] (BYU) in Provo, [[Utah]]. He joined BYU as an assistant professor in 2000 and has been a full professor since 2012. His research spans [[X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy]] (XPS), Fourier methods for spectral denoising and data science, [[spectroscopic ellipsometry]], surface modification and characterization, [[liquid chromatography|chromatographic]] materials, and long-term [[optical data storage]]. He has more than 550 publications and over 17,000 citations.<ref name="scholar">{{Cite web |title=Matthew Linford — Google Scholar Profile |url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=B2s-TsYAAAAJ&hl=en |access-date=2026-05-12}}</ref>

==Academic background and career==
Linford received a Bachelor of Science in chemistry ''magna cum laude'' from Brigham Young University in 1990. He completed a Master of Science in Materials Science and Engineering and a Doctor of Philosophy in chemistry at [[Stanford University]] in 1996, where he was advised by [[Christopher E. D. Chidsey]]. His doctoral research produced the first two published papers on alkyl monolayers on hydrogen-terminated silicon surfaces;<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Linford |first1=M. R. |last2=Chidsey |first2=C. E. D. |title=Alkyl monolayers covalently bonded to silicon surfaces |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |year=1993 |volume=115 |issue=26 |pages=12631–12632 |doi=10.1021/ja00070a008}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Linford |first1=M. R. |last2=Fenter |first2=P. |last3=Eisenberger |first3=P. M. |last4=Chidsey |first4=C. E. D. |title=Alkyl monolayers on silicon prepared from 1-alkenes and hydrogen-terminated silicon |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |year=1995 |volume=117 |issue=11 |pages=3145–3155 |doi=10.1021/ja00116a019}}</ref> those papers have accumulated more than 950 and 1,450 citations respectively. During graduate study he held a [[Fannie and John Hertz Foundation|Hertz Fellowship]] from 1991 to 1996, one of the most competitive fellowships in the physical sciences and engineering in the United States.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Hertz Fellows Directory |url=https://www.hertzfoundation.org/hertz-community/fellows-directory/ |access-date=2026-05-12 |website=Hertz Foundation}}</ref> He conducted postdoctoral research at the Max Planck Institute for Colloids and Interfaces in Germany from 1996 to 1997, where he worked with Helmut Möhwald on polyelectrolyte multilayers.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Matthew Linford |url=https://science.byu.edu/directory/matthew-linford |access-date=2026-05-12 |website=The College of Physical and Mathematical Sciences (CPMS) |language=en}}</ref>

Linford joined BYU as an assistant professor in 2000 and became a full professor in 2012. As of 2024, his Google Scholar profile lists more than 17,120 citations, an h-index of 57, and an i10-index of 230.<ref name="scholar"/> He has approximately 550 publications, including peer-reviewed papers, book chapters, conference proceedings, peer-reviewed contributions to spectral databases, tutorial articles, and more than 40 patents.

His research group has worked on XPS peak fitting, Fourier-domain denoising of spectral data, [[spectroscopic ellipsometry]], [[principal component analysis]] (PCA), [[multivariate curve resolution]] (MCR), [[atomic layer deposition]], new materials for [[liquid chromatography|chromatographic]] separations, [[chemomechanics|chemomechanical]] functionalization of silicon, and materials for long-term [[optical data storage]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Linford Research Group |url=https://labs.chem.byu.edu/linford-lab |access-date=2024-04-17 |website=Chemistry and Biochemistry Labs |language=en}}</ref> A 2025 paper in the ''[[Journal of Vacuum Science and Technology A]]'' established the peer-reviewed methodology underlying the group's Fourier-based XPS denoising approach.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The case for denoising (smoothing) X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) data |url=https://pubs.aip.org/avs/jva/article-abstract/43/3/033401/3339864/The-case-for-denoising-smoothing-X-ray?redirectedFrom=fulltext |access-date=2026-05-12 |website=Journal of Vacuum Science & Technology A |publisher=AIP Publishing}}</ref>

In 2015 Linford was named an Alcuin Fellow at Brigham Young University, an honor for outstanding teacher-scholars whose work transcends disciplinary boundaries.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Matthew Linford |url=https://science.byu.edu/directory/matthew-linford |access-date=2026-05-12 |website=The College of Physical and Mathematical Sciences (CPMS)}}</ref> He was named a Fellow of the [[American Vacuum Society]] (AVS) in 2014.<ref>[https://avs.org/Awards-Recognition/Society-Honors/Fellow-of-the-Society Fellow of the Society] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160314034305/http://avs.org/Awards-Recognition/Society-Honors/Fellow-of-the-Society |date=2016-03-14}}. [[American Vacuum Society]]. Retrieved October 28, 2014.</ref>

Linford has been a contributing editor for ''Vacuum Technology & Coating'' since 2014, for which he has authored more than 100 columns on surface and material characterization. He served as an editor for ''Applied Surface Science'' ([[Elsevier]]) from 2015 to 2023, handling more than 1,600 manuscripts. He was an associate editor of ''Surface Science Spectra'' from 2003 to 2019 and joined its editorial board in 2019. He also serves on the editorial boards of ''Separations'' and ''Hybrid Advances''.

==Industrial experience==
Prior to joining BYU, Linford worked in industry for three years. As a senior scientist at Rohm and Haas Company (1997–1998), he developed an infrared tool for rapid catalyst screening and designed a laser scanner for detecting defects in plastic sheets used as flat panel display substrates. As a senior scientist at Praelux, Inc. (1998–1999), he developed methods to immobilize nucleotides and DNA oligomers onto surfaces and procedures to attach nickel NTA chelators to glass coverslips for 6-His-tagged protein binding.{{citation needed|date=May 2026}}

As director of research at Nano-Tex, LLC (1999–2000), Linford developed the product "Nano-Dry," a hydrophobic treatment that makes nylon and polyester more hydrophilic and comfortable to wear. The product was marketed nationally and became part of the Nike golf collection; [[Tiger Woods]] is shown wearing pants with the Nano-Dry finish in the October 2003 issue of ''[[Golf Digest]]''. He was named as inventor on more than 10 patents from his work at Nano-Tex.{{citation needed|date=May 2026}}

==Companies founded==
Linford has co-founded several companies:

* '''Laser Array Technologies''' (2006–2011) developed microlens laser patterning of surfaces for bioarray fabrication.
* '''Millenniata, Inc.''' (founded 2007) developed [[M-DISC]], a write-once optical disc technology. The company produced a DVD rated for more than 1,000 years of data retention and a Blu-ray disc rated for at least 300 years; the products were sold commercially by [[Verbatim (brand)|Verbatim]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.millenniata.com/ |title=Home |website=millenniata.com}}</ref> Linford served on Millenniata's board from June 2007 to April 2010.
* '''Xeromax, Inc.''' (2009–2011) received the "Outstanding Product" award at the Global Moot Corp competition at the [[University of Texas at Austin]] in 2009, as well as First Place at the BYU Business Plan Competition and Second Place at the Wake Forest Elevator Pitch Competition.
* '''NanoXCoatings and NanoXChromatography''' (founded 2020) licensed BYU-developed chromatography technology; their diamond-based high-performance liquid chromatography column was sold by Diamond Analytics.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Self-Assembled Nanomaterials for Enhanced Chemical Separations |url=https://www.chromatographyonline.com/view/self-assembled-nanomaterials-enhanced-chemical-separations |access-date=2026-05-12 |website=Chromatography Online}}</ref>
* '''Fourier-AI Innovations, LLC''' (founded 2026) is a BYU spinout developing software for automated Fourier-domain denoising of XPS spectra, including the patent-pending Binary Residual Map™ visualization tool.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Fourier-AI Innovations |url=https://fourier-ai.com/ |access-date=2026-05-12}}</ref>
